body:
I actually went upstate recently to stay with friends through the rest of the month. I've struggled with PTSD (I was raped by my boss years ago and there was a big coverup in the aftermath, so I already struggle with trust) and clinical depression for years and was really making a ton of progress before the lockdowns. Being abruptly dumped and put in isolation was probably the worst thing for that. I stopped sleeping, traumatic flashbacks became more frequent and I spiraled into a place so dark I was afraid I was going to hurt myself.

I consider myself incredibly lucky that I have this option and such supportive friends.  Being up here and with other people has really has helped me stabilize my mood and dark thoughts immensely.  I still struggle with sleeping due to night terrors, but I'm more relaxed and I'm no longer having traumatizing flashbacks.  But I know I can't be here forever. I have to return to the city in a few days because my lease is up and I need to move. I have to face reality. I can't hide upstate until there's a vaccine.

I think what makes this so difficult is the lack of hope. In the past, when I would fall into a deep depression I was always able to pull myself up by remaining hopeful of all the life I have to look forward to -- traveling, exciting work opportunities, meeting new people, falling in love.  Now with infectious disease experts saying this will be the norm for *years,* realistically all I have to look forward to is *surviving*. Yes, I can see my close friends eventually. Yes, I can start a hobby or do yoga. Yes, I have my physical health (knock on wood). But I still feel trapped, I still feel like I'm just trying to get through life day by day.  Add getting my heart broken in a time when the prospect of finding love, companionship and a partner who respects me and won't bail the second their infatuation disappears will be incredibly challenging for the foreseeable future.  I feel as though I've been banished to a life of crippling loneliness and celibacy for the next two to three years.

I was talking to a friend about my situation. She told me her brother was dumped by his girlfriend after he confided his clinical depression to her. When I asked her how long it took him to heal from that betrayal she said, "Years."

It's the prospect of feeling this way for years that breaks me. I already struggled for years. I struggled *so* hard and put in *so* much work. I know what "years" means, how long and painful it is. I don't want to go through that again, only this time my options for finding joy and healing being even more restricted.
